headings.title: Introduction to Healthcare Resource Management
headings.content: Managing drugs and medical supplies is a core responsibility for nurses across every clinical setting. Without proper oversight, wards quickly face stockouts of essential items like 5% dextrose, syringes, and basic antibiotics, directly compromising patient safety. Resource management bridges clinical care and administrative efficiency. Nurses act as the primary gatekeepers of these assets because they use them daily at the bedside. Understanding basic economic and organizational principles helps minimize waste and ensures that public health facilities stretch limited budgets to serve more patients.

headings.title: Classification and Identification of Drugs and Medical Supplies
headings.content:
A well-organized treatment room relies on clear categorization of items. Drugs and supplies are grouped to prevent dangerous medication errors and speed up retrieval during emergencies.

- **Consumables**: Single-use items like cotton balls, gauze, examination gloves, and disposable syringes.
- **Durable Equipment**: Reusable tools such as stethoscope heads, blood pressure cuffs, and surgical scissors.
- **Emergency Pharmaceuticals**: Life-saving injectables like adrenaline, atropine, and hydrocortisone, kept together in a designated crash cart.
- **Controlled Substances**: Highly regulated medications like pethidine and morphine that require double-locking and strict tallying.

headings.title: Inventory Control Systems and Stock Management
headings.content:
Keeping track of stock prevents both running out of vital items and hoarding supplies that might expire on the shelf. Effective inventory management relies on systematic monitoring of stock levels.

- **Maximum Stock Level**: The highest permitted quantity of an item that a ward should hold without causing waste or storage issues.
- **Minimum Stock Level**: The baseline safety threshold that triggers a reorder before supplies run completely dry.
- **Lead Time**: The duration it takes from placing an order with the central medical store until the items physically arrive on the ward.
- **Buffer Stock**: An extra reserve of supplies kept on hand to handle sudden patient surges or unexpected delivery delays.

headings.title: Storage, Handling, and Maintenance Guidelines
headings.content: Drugs and medical supplies lose their potency or become contaminated if stored improperly. Environmental factors like heat, direct sunlight, and humidity degrade chemical compounds rapidly. Most routine pharmaceuticals require storage in cool, dry, and well-ventilated rooms, while vaccines and certain antibiotics demand strict cold-chain maintenance inside pharmaceutical refrigerators. Ward refrigerators must be monitored daily with recorded temperature logs. Furthermore, heavy supplies should never be stacked so high that they risk toppling over and injuring staff.

headings.title: Dispensing, Administration, and Waste Control
headings.content: Ensuring safe delivery of medication from the pharmacy shelf to the patient requires strict adherence to safety checks. Nurses must practice the rights of medication administration while also watching out for unused or partially used drugs. When an injectable medication is drawn up but not given, it must be discarded safely according to hospital policy rather than saved for another patient. Waste management also extends to sharps safety; needles must never be recapped by hand before disposal in puncture-resistant safety boxes.

headings.title: Infection Control and Management of Expired Supplies
headings.content: Expired or damaged supplies pose a hidden hazard in clinical environments. A common misconception is that a drug is safe to use a few weeks past its expiration date; however, chemical degradation can produce toxic byproducts or weaken the active ingredient entirely. Ward stock must be organized using the **FEFO** principle—First Expire, First Out—meaning items that expire sooner are placed in front of newer stock. Damaged sterile packaging, such as a torn suture pouch or a cracked infusion set, must be treated as contaminated and discarded immediately.

headings.title: Auditing, Accountability, and Record Keeping
headings.content: Rigorous record-keeping establishes clear accountability for every drug and supply item entering or leaving the ward. Stock registers, bin cards, and narcotic logbooks must be updated immediately upon receipt or administration of any item. Discrepancies between physical counts and written records should be investigated without delay to deter theft or loss. Regular internal audits protect nursing staff by proving that resources are handled transparently and in full compliance with institutional standards.
